theme: You are mine; the only God; Cyrus named
readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 43:1-45:25. God declares that he is the only God, he promises to redeem Israel, and he names Cyrus, a pagan king, as his instrument more than a century before he was born. Read with attention to the repeated “I am the LORD.”
settingTheScene: The exiles in Babylon thought that their God had been defeated by the gods of Babylon. Isaiah answers that God is not only sovereign but alone. The chapters here contain some of the strongest statements of monotheism in the Bible. They also contain the astonishing prophecy that Cyrus of Persia, who conquered Babylon in 539 BC, would be God’s shepherd to free his people.
observation: “Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine” (43:1).
“When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you” (43:2).
“I, I am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior” (43:11).
“Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it springs forth, do you not perceive it?” (43:19).
“I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins” (43:25).
“Before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me” (43:10).
“Who says of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose” (44:28).
“Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other” (45:22).
interpretation:
Chapter 43 opens with “But now.” After the discipline of exile, God speaks. “Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine.” Notice the order: redemption first, then the claim. Israel is his because he bought them. Then the promises: through the waters, the rivers, the fire. These echo the sea and the Jordan. He will gather them from the ends of the earth.

God then argues against the idols. The nations are summoned to a court. Who among them declared the things that would happen? Israel is God’s witness: “You are my witnesses… and my servant whom I have chosen.” There is only one God and one Savior. The strongest part comes next. Though Israel has not called on him, wearied him with sins, and burdened him with iniquities, “I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins.” Forgiveness comes from God’s own initiative, not from Israel’s merit.

Chapter 44 contains a famous satire on idolatry. A man cuts down a tree, burns half for warming himself and cooking, and carves the rest into a god and bows down to it. “Deliver me, for you are my god!” Isaiah exposes the foolishness: it is a lie in his right hand. In contrast, the LORD says, “I formed you; you are my servant; O Israel, I will not forget you.”

At the end of chapter 44 and in chapter 45, Cyrus is named. God calls him “my shepherd” and “his anointed.” A pagan king who does not know the LORD is used for God’s purposes. This shows that God is sovereign over history, even over those who do not acknowledge him. God’s purpose is that people “may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me.”

The invitation at the end of chapter 45 is a gospel call: “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth!” One day every knee will bow.
connection: Philippians 2:10-11 quotes Isaiah 45:23: every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. Revelation 2:17 and John 10:3 echo God’s calling us by name. Acts 4:12 says there is salvation in no one else. Hebrews 8:12 says that God will remember our sins no more. 2 Corinthians 5:17 speaks of the new creation: “the old has passed away; behold, the new has come.” Romans 9:20-21 draws on the potter and clay imagery of Isaiah 45:9.
application:
Say aloud Isaiah 43:1 as a statement about you: “I have called you by name, you are mine.”

Notice a “new thing” that God may be doing in your life. Ask for eyes to see it.

Reflect on “Cyrus.” How has God used people who do not know him to serve you?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that you are called by name and are his.
Thank him that he is with you in the waters.
Thank him for blotting out your transgressions.
